processing: Sun-dried sheng maocha from old trees in forest surroundings, kept loose or pressed, with no ripe-style fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring old-tree leaf is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: As is typical of Yiwu old-tree tea, long, sturdy dark-green strands with pale buds.
appearance_liquor: Rich, clear gold that holds its colour across steeps.
taste_profile: Wilder and broader than most Yiwu, with a substantial body, sweet honeyed fragrance and the soft texture Yiwu is known for.

brewing.notes: Strong for Yiwu, so do not overdo the leaf. Short early steeps show the fragrance, and it holds up over many rounds.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as sheng, young or lightly aged, and old-tree spring tea takes the top price. A published spring price index listed village-side small trees at 400 to 500 yuan per kilogram and old trees at 1,000 to 1,600. Laotian maocha is commonly passed off as Guafengzhai, so the source matters more than the wrapper.
description:
Guafengzhai is a remote, purely Yao village on the Laos border at the eastern edge of Mengla County, about 31 kilometres from the township seat. Its name means windy village, and it has become one of the most sought-after names in the Yiwu area.

The tea grows among a large area of primary forest, across the Lengshui river from Dingjiazhai, and the area has many old trees. It is made in the usual sheng way, so the place does the work.

In the cup it is stronger than most of Yiwu, wild and broad, but it keeps the region's fragrance and soft texture. Keep early steeps short and use a little less leaf than for a gentler Yiwu; it will last for many rounds.

Fakes are the main issue. Laotian leaf is regularly sold through the village as local tea, so a suspiciously cheap old-tree cake usually explains itself. Buy from people who can tell you which plot, Chawangshu for example, and who made it.
history:
The village became known to tea drinkers only after 2007, when mountain-specific pu-erh grew popular; until then it was simply one of the remote settlements of the Yiwu area, listed among its eight stockaded villages and within the old Gumansa mountain.

Fame brought problems. The price of old-tree leaf rose, and with it the trade in Laotian tea brought over the nearby border and sold under the village name.
